usage: The set phrase Koreans use to distinguish an old open-air market from a modern store; 전통 = 'tradition'.
에 marks the destination you move toward; pair it with movement verbs 가다/오다/다니다.
에서 marks where an action takes place; here the buying happens inside the market.
An idiom: 시장(을) 보다 literally 'see the market' but means to go shopping for groceries — note 보다, not 사다.
examples: 시장이 커요.
The market is big.
A bare description; subject particle 이 after a consonant. Start simple.
주말마다 전통 시장에서 과일을 사요.
Every weekend I buy fruit at the traditional market.
마다 = 'every'; 에서 because the buying happens at the market, not 에.
시장에 가면 깎아 달라고 해 보세요.
When you go to the market, try asking them to knock the price down.
깎다 = 'cut/discount the price' — real bargaining only happens at 시장, not at a fixed-price 마트.
nuance: 시장 (市場, 'market-place/field') is an open traditional market: rows of small independent stalls selling produce, fish, side dishes and clothes, where prices are flexible and you can haggle. The dividing line from its near-synonym 마트 is atmosphere and pricing — 마트 is a single fixed-price corporate store, while 시장 is many vendors and bargaining (깎다) is normal. Don't confuse it with 장 alone (which in 장을 보다 / 장날 means the shopping or market-day event) or with the homophone 시장 (市長, 'mayor'); only context tells them apart. The classic English-speaker trap is the particle: you say 시장에 가요 for *going there* (에 = destination) but 시장에서 사요 for *buying there* (에서 = where the action happens), and English 'go shopping' becomes the fixed idiom 시장을 보다, using 보다 'see', never 사다.

市場 means 'market-place/field'.

The classic English-speaker trap is the particle: you say 시장에 가요 for going there (에 = destination) but 시장에서 사요 for buying there (에서 = where the action happens), and English 'go shopping' becomes the fixed idiom 시장을 보다, using 보다 'see', never 사다.

mistakes: Saying 시장에서 가요 for 'I go to the market'. With the movement verb 가다 you need the destination particle 에 (시장에 가요); 에서 would wrongly mean an action performed *at* the market.
Translating 'go shopping' word-for-word as 시장을 사요. The fixed expression is 시장을 보다 ('see the market'); 사다 needs a specific object like 과일을 사요.
Mixing up 시장(市場, market) and 시장(市長, mayor) because they sound identical. They are different words; rely on context — 시장에 가다 = market, 시장님 = mayor.

usage: 대형 = 'large-scale'; the standard label for hypermarket chains like 이마트 or 홈플러스.
에 marks the destination; use with 가다/오다 when you mean heading there.
I do the grocery shopping at the supermarket
에서 = where the action happens; 장(을) 보다 is the everyday idiom for 'grocery-shop'.
동네 = 'neighborhood'; a smaller local 마트, between a 대형 마트 and a corner 가게.
examples: 마트가 가까워요.
The supermarket is close.
Simple description; 가깝다 'to be near'. Note 가 after the vowel-final 마트.
저녁에 마트에서 우유랑 빵을 샀어요.
In the evening I bought milk and bread at the supermarket.
랑 = casual 'and' for listing items; 에서 because the buying is done there.
주말에는 마트가 너무 붐벼서 평일에 장을 봐요.
On weekends the supermarket is too crowded, so I shop on weekdays.
붐비다 'to be crowded'; ~아서/어서 gives the reason.
nuance: 마트 is a clipped loanword from English 'mart', meaning a large modern self-service supermarket or discount store — typically a chain (이마트, 홈플러스, 롯데마트) with fixed prices, shopping carts and barcodes. The line against its synonyms is size and pricing: 시장 is many haggling stalls, a 가게 is a tiny single shop, a 편의점 is a small 24-hour store, while 마트 is a big one-stop store where you 장을 보다 ('do a grocery run'). Because it is borrowed, there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, English 'mart' is rare, so learners under-use this very common word and over-reach with 슈퍼마켓 (Koreans usually just say 마트 or the older 슈퍼); second, the particle split — 마트에 가요 for going there but 마트에서 사요 for buying there — and don't say 마트를 봐요; the grocery idiom attaches to 장, i.e. 장을 봐요.

mistakes: Calling a tiny corner store a 마트. A small always-open shop is a 편의점 and a little independent store is a 가게; 마트 implies a large supermarket with carts and many aisles.
Saying 마트를 봐요 for 'I shop at the supermarket'. The shopping idiom is 장을 보다, so it is 마트에서 장을 봐요 — the object is 장, and the location takes 에서.
Defaulting to 슈퍼마켓 in every sentence. It is understood but stiff; natural speech uses 마트 (big store) or 슈퍼 (small local grocery).

usage: 도시락 = packed meal; a cheap ready-to-eat box, a staple of Korean 편의점 culture.
I go to the convenience store
에 marks the destination with movement verbs 가다/오다.
I buy (it) at the convenience store
에서 marks the place of the action; the buying happens inside the store.
24시간 = 'open around the clock'; the defining feature of a 편의점.
examples: 편의점이 많아요.
There are many convenience stores.
Basic existence statement; 많다 'to be many'. 이 after a consonant.
밤늦게 편의점에서 라면을 사 먹었어요.
Late at night I bought ramen at the convenience store and ate it.
사 먹다 'buy and eat' is one chunk; 에서 marks where it happened.
편의점에서 택배도 보내고 공과금도 낼 수 있어요.
At the convenience store you can also send parcels and pay utility bills.
~을 수 있다 'can'; shows the real range of services beyond snacks.
nuance: 편의점 (便宜店, 'convenience-store', 便宜 'convenient' + 店 'store') is the small, brightly lit, usually 24-hour chain store on every Korean corner — CU, GS25, 세븐일레븐, 이마트24. The contrast with its neighbors is scale and price: it is far smaller than a 마트, more expensive per item, but always open and packed with ready meals, drinks and services (parcel pickup, bill payment, ATM, cash withdrawal). It also differs from a plain 가게 in that 가게 is an independent mom-and-pop shop while 편의점 is a branded chain. Note the hanja 便宜: in Korean 편의 means 'convenience', though the same characters read 便宜 in Chinese mean 'cheap' — a false-friend trap if you know Chinese. The everyday English-speaker error is the destination/location particle (편의점에 가요 vs 편의점에서 사요) and assuming it only sells snacks; in Korea the 편의점 is a genuine errand hub.

structuredNuance.t: 편의점 is the small, brightly lit, usually 24-hour chain store on every Korean corner — CU, GS25, 세븐일레븐, 이마트24. It is packed with ready meals, drinks and services (parcel pickup, bill payment, ATM, cash withdrawal); in Korea the 편의점 is a genuine errand hub, not just a snack stop.

便宜店 = 便宜 'convenient' + 店 'store'. In Korean 편의 means 'convenience', though the same characters read 便宜 in Chinese mean 'cheap' — a false-friend trap if you know Chinese.
The everyday error is the destination/location particle (편의점에 가요 vs 편의점에서 사요) and assuming it only sells snacks.

mistakes: Calling a big supermarket a 편의점. Size and price differ: a large multi-aisle store with carts is a 마트, while 편의점 is a small 24-hour corner store.
If you know Chinese, reading 편의(便宜) as 'cheap'. In Korean these characters mean 'convenience'; 편의점 is named for being handy, not for low prices (it is actually pricier than a 마트).
Saying 편의점에서 가요 for 'I go to the convenience store'. Movement to a place takes 에 (편의점에 가요); 에서 is only for an action done there, like 편의점에서 사요.

usage: 조용하다 'to be quiet'; 조용한 카페 is a prized spot for studying or talking.
에 marks the destination you head to with 가다/오다.
에서 marks where the activity happens; people study and work in Korean cafes for hours.
투어 from 'tour'; visiting several trendy cafes in a day, a popular outing.
examples: 카페가 예뻐요.
The cafe is pretty.
Simple description; 예쁘다 here praises the interior/atmosphere, a very common reason to pick a cafe.
친구랑 카페에서 두 시간 동안 수다 떨었어요.
I chatted with a friend at the cafe for two hours.
동안 = 'for (a duration)'; 수다(를) 떨다 'to chat away' — cafes are social hubs.
이 카페는 자리도 넓고 콘센트도 많아서 일하기 좋아요.
This cafe has roomy seats and lots of outlets, so it's good for working.
콘센트 = power outlet; ~기 좋다 'good for ~ing' explains why Koreans 'cafe-work'.
nuance: 카페 is a loanword (from French/English 'café') meaning a coffee shop — but in Korea it is as much a social and study space as a place to drink coffee; people sit for hours to chat, work on laptops, or go on a 카페 투어 of photogenic spots. The key contrast learners blur is 카페 vs 커피: 카페 is the *place*, 커피 is the *drink*, so '커피 마시러 카페에 가요' (go to the cafe to drink coffee). It overlaps with 커피숍 and the older 다방 (a dated tea-room), but 카페 is the modern default. Being borrowed, it has no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 카페/커피 mix-up, plus the particles — 카페에 가요 for going there but 카페에서 공부해요 for doing something there — and remember the purpose marker for 'to go drink coffee' is the verb stem + ~(으)러: 커피 마시러 카페에 가요.

카페 is a loanword (from French/English 'café'). Being borrowed, it has no hanja.

The pitfall is exactly that 카페/커피 mix-up, plus the particles — 카페에 가요 for going there but 카페에서 공부해요 for doing something there — and remember the purpose marker for 'to go drink coffee' is the verb stem + ~(으)러: 커피 마시러 카페에 가요.

Using 에 instead of 에서 for activities done inside: 카페에 공부해요 is wrong. An action performed at the cafe takes 에서 — 카페에서 공부해요.
Assuming a 카페 only sells coffee fast like a takeout stand. Korean cafes are sit-down social/study spaces; ordering one drink and staying for hours is normal and expected.

usage: 직원 = staff member; the person at the counter who handles your transaction.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
I withdraw money at the bank
에서 = location of the action; note 돈을 찾다 'find money' = 'withdraw', an idiom.
계좌 (口座) = account; 계좌를 열다/만들다 'open an account', a first task for newcomers.
examples: 은행이 멀어요.
The bank is far.
Simple distance description; 멀다 'to be far'. 이 after a consonant.
은행에서 통장을 만들었어요.
I opened a bankbook at the bank.
통장 = passbook/account; 에서 because the action is done at the bank.
은행은 보통 네 시에 문을 닫으니까 일찍 가세요.
Banks usually close at four, so go early.
~(으)니까 gives a reason for advice; 문을 닫다 'close (the doors)'.
nuance: 은행 (銀行, literally 'silver-shop/row', 銀 'silver' + 行 'shop/business') is a bank handling savings, transfers, currency exchange and accounts — a critical first stop for newcomers needing a 계좌 (account) and 통장 (bankbook). Two things trip up English speakers. First, the verb for 'withdraw' is the idiom 돈을 찾다 — literally 'to find money' — not 빼다 or a literal 'withdraw'; conversely 'deposit' is 돈을 넣다 'put money in'. Second, watch the homophone-ish 은행(銀杏) meaning 'ginkgo (nut/tree)': written and pronounced almost the same, distinguished only by context (은행에 가다 = bank; 은행나무 = ginkgo tree). As always, 은행에 가요 marks the destination (에) while 은행에서 돈을 찾아요 marks where the action occurs (에서); the direct English calque 'I go at the bank' with 에서 is the classic slip.

structuredNuance.t: 은행 is a bank handling savings, transfers, currency exchange and accounts — a critical first stop for newcomers needing a 계좌 (account) and 통장 (bankbook).

銀行 literally means 'silver-shop/row': 銀 'silver' + 行 'shop/business'. Watch the homophone-ish 은행(銀杏) meaning 'ginkgo (nut/tree)': written and pronounced almost the same, distinguished only by context (은행에 가다 = bank; 은행나무 = ginkgo tree).

First, the verb for 'withdraw' is the idiom 돈을 찾다 — literally 'to find money' — not 빼다 or a literal 'withdraw'; conversely 'deposit' is 돈을 넣다 'put money in'. Second, 은행에 가요 marks the destination (에) while 은행에서 돈을 찾아요 marks where the action occurs (에서); the direct English calque 'I go at the bank' with 에서 is the classic slip.

mistakes: Saying 돈을 빼요 or a literal 'withdraw' verb for taking money out. Korean uses the idiom 돈을 찾다 ('find money') for withdrawing, and 돈을 넣다 ('put money in') for depositing.
Writing 은행에서 가요 for 'I go to the bank'. Going to a place uses 에 (은행에 가요); 에서 marks an action done there, e.g. 은행에서 돈을 찾아요.
Confusing 은행(銀行, bank) with 은행(銀杏, ginkgo). They sound nearly identical; context decides — 은행 계좌 = bank account, but 은행나무 / 은행을 줍다 = ginkgo tree / picking up ginkgo nuts.

usage: 넓다 'to be wide/spacious'; describes the open green area itself.
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.
I take a walk in the park
에서 = where the action happens; 산책(을) 하다 'to take a stroll' is the classic park activity.
벤치 from 'bench'; 벤치에 앉다 'sit on the bench' — note location 에 with the static verb 앉다.
examples: 공원이 넓어요.
The park is spacious.
Basic description; 넓다 'to be wide'. 이 after a consonant.
저녁마다 공원에서 강아지랑 산책해요.
Every evening I walk the dog in the park.
마다 'every'; 에서 because the walking happens in the park; 랑 'with' (casual).
주말에는 공원에서 돗자리 깔고 도시락 먹는 사람이 많아요.
On weekends many people lay out a mat and eat lunchboxes in the park.
돗자리(를) 깔다 'spread a picnic mat' — a very Korean park scene; 에서 marks the location.
nuance: 공원 (公園, 'public-garden', 公 'public' + 園 'garden') is a public green space for walking, exercise, picnics and rest — found in every Korean neighborhood, from small 근린공원 to huge ones like 한강공원 or 올림픽공원. The near-synonym to distinguish is 정원 (庭園), a private *garden* attached to a home or building: 공원 is open to everyone, 정원 is someone's own landscaped yard, so don't call a public park a 정원. It is also not 놀이공원 (an amusement park with rides) — that compound needs 놀이. The collocations are scenic: 공원에서 산책하다 (stroll), 운동하다 (exercise), 돗자리를 깔다 (spread a picnic mat). The English-speaker pitfall is again 공원에 가요 (destination, 에) versus 공원에서 산책해요 (action location, 에서); and the static verb 앉다 takes 에 — 벤치에 앉다 'sit on the bench', not 에서.

The near-synonym to distinguish is 정원 (庭園), a private garden attached to a home or building: 공원 is open to everyone, 정원 is someone's own landscaped yard, so don't call a public park a 정원. It is also not 놀이공원 (an amusement park with rides) — that compound needs 놀이.
公園 means 'public-garden': 公 'public' + 園 'garden'.
The pitfall is again 공원에 가요 (destination, 에) versus 공원에서 산책해요 (action location, 에서); and the static verb 앉다 takes 에 — 벤치에 앉다 'sit on the bench', not 에서.

mistakes: Calling a private home garden a 공원. 공원 is a *public* green space; a private landscaped yard is a 정원 (庭園). The 公 in 공원 literally means 'public'.
Saying 공원에서 가요 for 'I go to the park'. Movement to the park needs 에 (공원에 가요); 에서 only marks an action carried out there, like 공원에서 운동해요.
Using 공원 to mean an amusement park. Rides-and-attractions parks are 놀이공원 (e.g. 에버랜드는 놀이공원이에요); a plain 공원 is just a green park.

usage: 지하철 'subway' + 역; the most common compound, since urban Koreans live by subway lines.
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.
에서 = where the meeting happens; stations are the default Korean meeting point.
출구 (出口) = exit; Koreans navigate by exit number — '3번 출구에서 만나' ('meet at exit 3').
examples: 역이 가까워요.
The station is close.
Simple description; 가깝다 'to be near'. A big plus when renting a room.
서울역에서 기차를 탔어요.
I took the train at Seoul Station.
서울역 = Seoul Station; 에서 because boarding happens at the station; 타다 'to ride/board'.
3번 출구로 나와서 역 앞에서 기다릴게요.
I'll come out of exit 3 and wait in front of the station.
~(으)로 나오다 'come out via'; 앞에서 'in front of' + 에서 marks the waiting spot.
nuance: 역 (驛, 'relay station / post-horse stage') means a train or subway station and almost always attaches to a place or line name — 서울역, 강남역, 부산역. It is the everyday navigation anchor of Korean city life, with people meeting and giving directions by 출구 (exit) number. Distinguish it from 정류장 (停留場), which is a *bus stop* — buses stop at a 버스 정류장, not a 역, so don't mix them. The historical hanja 驛 refers to old relay-horse posts, now repurposed for rail. Beware two look-alikes: 역할 (役割, 'role') and the particle/adverb 역시 ('as expected') share the syllable 역 but are unrelated words. The reliable English-speaker error is particles: 역에 가요 for going to the station (에 = destination) but 역에서 만나요 / 기차를 타요 for an action at the station (에서); never say 역에서 가요 when you mean 'go there'.

structuredNuance.t: 역 means a train or subway station and almost always attaches to a place or line name — 서울역, 강남역, 부산역. It is the everyday navigation anchor of Korean city life, with people meeting and giving directions by 출구 (exit) number.

Distinguish it from 정류장 (停留場), which is a bus stop — buses stop at a 버스 정류장, not a 역, so don't mix them. Beware two look-alikes too: 역할 (役割, 'role') and the particle/adverb 역시 ('as expected') share the syllable 역 but are unrelated words.
驛 means 'relay station / post-horse stage'; the historical hanja refers to old relay-horse posts, now repurposed for rail.
The reliable error is particles: 역에 가요 for going to the station (에 = destination) but 역에서 만나요 / 기차를 타요 for an action at the station (에서); never say 역에서 가요 when you mean 'go there'.

mistakes: Calling a bus stop a 역. Trains and subways stop at a 역, but buses stop at a 정류장 (버스 정류장). 'I'll wait at the bus stop' = 버스 정류장에서 기다릴게요, not 역에서.
Saying 역에서 가요 for 'I go to the station'. Going there takes 에 (역에 가요); 에서 is for an action done at the station, e.g. 역에서 만나요.
Confusing 역(驛, station) with 역할(役割, role). They share one syllable but are different words: 강남역 = Gangnam Station, but 역할이 중요해요 = 'the role is important'.

usage: 가깝다 'to be near'; handy when you need to mail something quickly.
I go to the post office
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
I mail it at the post office
에서 = where the action happens; 부치다 'to send/mail (a parcel or letter)'.
택배 (宅配) = home-delivery service; the post office's parcel-shipping option, often cheaper than private couriers.
examples: 우체국이 어디예요?
Where is the post office?
Basic question with 어디 'where'; 이 after a consonant. Essential newcomer phrase.
우체국에서 소포를 부쳤어요.
I mailed a parcel at the post office.
소포 'parcel' + 부치다 'to send'; 에서 marks where the sending was done.
우체국에서 국제 택배 보내면 일주일쯤 걸려요.
If you send an international parcel from the post office, it takes about a week.
~(으)면 'if/when'; 걸리다 'to take (time)'; 쯤 'about'. Practical mailing info.
nuance: 우체국 (郵遞局, 'mail-deliver-bureau': 郵 'post/mail' + 遞 'deliver/relay' + 局 'bureau/office') is the post office — it handles letters, parcels (소포), home-delivery 택배, and also some banking and bill payments through 우체국 (the postal bank). The verb you need is 부치다 'to send/mail', as in 편지를 부치다 / 소포를 부치다; be careful not to confuse it with the homophone 부치다 'to fry (a pancake)' or with 붙이다 'to stick/attach' — same sound, different spelling and meaning. Distinguish 우체국 from 은행: while the post office offers limited banking, money matters proper belong to a 은행, and parcels belong to the 우체국. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual particle pair — 우체국에 가요 (destination, 에) versus 우체국에서 부쳐요 (action location, 에서) — plus reaching for a literal 'send' verb instead of the idiomatic 부치다 for mail.

mistakes: Going to a 은행 to send a parcel. Banking-proper is the 은행's job, but mailing letters and parcels (소포/택배) is done at the 우체국.

usage: 가깝다 'to be near'; useful when deciding where to catch a film.
I go to the movie theater
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.
I watch a movie at the theater
에서 = where the action happens; note 영화를 보다 'watch a movie', the verb is 보다 'see'.
매점 (賣店) = snack stand; where you buy 팝콘 and drinks before the show.
examples: 영화관이 커요.
The movie theater is big.
Simple description; 크다 'to be big'. 이 after a consonant.
주말에 영화관에서 새 영화를 봤어요.
On the weekend I watched a new movie at the theater.
에서 because the watching happens at the theater; 영화를 보다 'watch a movie'.
요즘은 영화관에 안 가고 집에서 영화를 봐요.
These days I don't go to the theater; I watch movies at home.
Contrast with ~고 'and'; shows 영화관 (the building) vs watching 영화 (the film) anywhere.
nuance: 영화관 (映畵館, 'movie-hall': 映 'project/reflect' + 畵 'picture' + 館 'large building/hall') is the building where you watch films — the multiplexes CGV, 롯데시네마, 메가박스. The synonym 극장 (劇場, 'theater') historically means a stage/playhouse but is also used loosely for cinemas; 영화관 specifically means a *movie* theater, while 극장 can cover live-performance theaters too. The crucial contrast is 영화관 (the *place*/building) versus 영화 (the *film* itself): you 영화관에 가요 (go to the theater) to 영화를 봐요 (watch a movie), so don't say 영화에 가요. Note 영화를 보다 uses 보다 'see/watch', never 듣다 or a literal 'watch'. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this place-vs-thing mix and the particle pair: 영화관에 가요 for going (에 = destination) but 영화관에서 영화를 봐요 for the action inside (에서).

mistakes: Saying 영화에 가요 for 'I go to the movie theater'. 영화 is the film; the building is 영화관, so it is 영화관에 가요 (and you go there to 영화를 보다).
Saying 영화관에 영화를 봐요 with the wrong particle. An action done inside takes 에서 — 영화관에서 영화를 봐요; 에 here would only mark the destination of movement.
Forgetting the verb 보다 for films. 'Watch a movie' is 영화를 보다 ('see a movie'), not a literal 'watch' verb; you 영화관에서 영화를 봐요.

usage: 깨끗하다 'to be clean'; a top concern when picking lodging.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
에서 = where the action happens; 자다 'to sleep' / 묵다 'to stay overnight'.
예약 (豫約) = booking; 예약(을) 하다 'to make a reservation', essential before a trip.
examples: 호텔이 비싸요.
The hotel is expensive.
Simple description; 비싸다 'to be expensive'. 이 after a consonant.
어제 호텔에서 하룻밤 묵었어요.
Yesterday I stayed one night at the hotel.
하룻밤 'one night'; 묵다 'to lodge/stay over', more precise than 자다 for travel.
호텔이 역에서 가까워서 짐 들고 다니기 편했어요.
The hotel was close to the station, so it was easy to get around with luggage.
역에서 가깝다 'close *from* the station' — note 에서 marks the reference point for distance.
nuance: 호텔 is a loanword (from English 'hotel') meaning paid short-term lodging for travelers, from budget to luxury. For staying overnight the precise verb is 묵다 ('to lodge'), e.g. 호텔에서 묵다, though everyday speech also uses 자다 ('sleep'). Distinguish it from other Korean lodging: a 모텔 (motel) is a cheaper, often by-the-hour place; a 여관/여인숙 is an older budget inn; a 게스트하우스 is a hostel; a 펜션 is a self-catering holiday house — so 호텔 is the mid-to-upmarket option specifically. It is temporary paid lodging, never your own home (집). Being borrowed, it has no hanja. The English-speaker pitfalls are: using 집 for a hotel stay; forgetting 묵다 and over-relying on 자다; and the particles — note that with distance, 역에서 가까운 호텔 means 'a hotel *near* the station', where 에서 marks the point you measure *from*, while 호텔에 가요 (destination 에) and 호텔에서 자요 (action 에서) keep the usual split.

mistakes: Calling your hotel stay 집. 호텔 is temporary paid lodging for travelers; 집 is your own home. 'I'm staying at a hotel' = 호텔에서 묵어요, not 집에서.
Using 자다 when 묵다 is more natural for travel lodging. 자다 just means 'sleep'; for staying overnight at accommodation, Koreans say 호텔에서 묵다 ('lodge at the hotel').
Saying 호텔에서 가까워요 to mean 'the hotel is close' on its own. 에서 here needs a reference point: 역에서 호텔이 가까워요 ('the hotel is close *from* the station'); without it, just say 호텔이 가까워요.

usage: 작다 'to be small'; 가게 typically implies a modest, independent store.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
에서 = where the action happens; the buying is done in the shop.
꽃 'flower' + 가게; 가게 freely compounds with goods — 빵 가게 (bakery), 옷 가게 (clothing shop).
examples: 가게가 작아요.
The shop is small.
Simple description; 작다 'to be small'. 가 after the vowel-final 가게.
집 앞 가게에서 우유를 샀어요.
I bought milk at the shop in front of my house.
집 앞 'in front of the house'; 에서 marks where the buying happened.
저 사장님이 가게를 삼십 년 동안 하셨어요.
That owner has run the shop for thirty years.
가게를 하다 'to run a shop'; 동안 'for (a period)'; honorific ~으셨 for the owner.
nuance: 가게 is the general native-Korean word for a small shop or store — usually an independent, owner-run place, and it compounds freely with what it sells: 꽃 가게 (florist), 빵 가게 (bakery), 옷 가게 (clothes shop), 반찬 가게 (side-dish shop). The contrasts matter: a 가게 is smaller and more personal than a 마트 (big chain supermarket), and unlike a 편의점 it is an independent shop rather than a branded 24-hour chain. The verb 가게를 하다 / 가게를 차리다 means 'to run / open a shop'. Being a pure Korean word, it has no hanja (its more formal Sino-Korean cousin is 상점 商店). The English-speaker pitfalls: don't stretch 가게 to a huge store — that is a 마트 or 백화점 (department store); and keep the particle split, 가게에 가요 for going there (에) versus 가게에서 사요 for buying there (에서). English 'go to the shops' as a general outing maps better onto 장 보러 가다 or 쇼핑하러 가다, not a literal 가게에 가다.

usage: 높다 'to be tall/high'; 빌딩 specifically implies a large, modern, multi-story structure.
에 marks the destination/goal with 들어가다 'to go in'.
에서 = where the action happens; offices inside take 에서 for activities.
숲 'forest'; a vivid set phrase for a dense cluster of tall buildings downtown.
examples: 빌딩이 높아요.
The building is tall.
Simple description; 높다 'to be tall'. 이 after a consonant.
저 빌딩에서 친구를 만났어요.
I met my friend in that building.
에서 because the meeting (an action) took place inside the building.
회사가 저 유리 빌딩 십오 층에 있어요.
My company is on the 15th floor of that glass building.
층 'floor'; 에 marks the static location 'on the floor' with 있다.
nuance: 빌딩 is a loanword (from English 'building') but narrower than English 'building': it means specifically a *large, modern, multi-story* structure — an office tower or commercial high-rise, as in 유리 빌딩 (glass tower) or the set phrase 빌딩 숲 ('a forest of buildings'). The contrast with synonyms is size and type: a small house is 집, never 빌딩; a general 'structure' is 건물 (建物), the broad Sino-Korean word that covers *any* building including small ones, while 빌딩 implies it is tall and imposing. So a two-story shop is a 건물, not a 빌딩. Being borrowed, it has no hanja (its umbrella term 건물 does: 建物 'build-thing'). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 빌딩 for every 'building' the way English does — default to 건물 for the neutral word — plus the particle split: 빌딩에 들어가요 / 십오 층에 있어요 (destination/static 에) versus 빌딩에서 일해요 (action inside, 에서).

Calling a house a 빌딩. A home is 집; 빌딩 is a large multi-story commercial structure. 'I live in that building' for a residential block is better with 건물 or 아파트.
Saying 빌딩에서 들어가요 for 'I enter the building'. Entering (movement toward a goal) takes 에 with 들어가다 (빌딩에 들어가요); 에서 marks an action done inside, like 빌딩에서 일해요.
